question: Can serial passaging (pour survivors into a fresh world, let it run, pour those survivors onward) act as artificial selection by migration and carry complexity or hardiness forward where a single pour cannot?
sourceFile: index.html (verified unmodified: git diff --stat -- index.html empty before and after the study)
background: Builds on studies/collision-ecology.json (v1.38): single archipelago->mainland pours lose the visitor founding lineage within about an hour, but donor genes cross into native lines via hybridization whenever donor and recipient mean hue sit within the game's 40-degree sexual-reproduction gate (hueDist<40 in step()).

protocol.bootstrap: browser pane opened via preview_start on file:///.../primordial-soup/index.html (renders as a live data: snapshot -- functions/RNG fully live, just not backed by file:// persistence, which was never needed since every world used initWorld(scn,seed) explicitly); viewport forced to 1280x720 via resize_window before the standard bootstrap block; R===334 verified after bootstrap.
protocol.pourMechanism: every pour executed exactly as the shipped shelfPour() does: payload={tag, cs:[{g,sg,br,bh}...]} built from harvested creature snapshots captured BEFORE the recipient world's initWorld() call, then logIv('collide',payload) immediately followed by collideArrive(payload). No creature array was ever hand-edited.
protocol.execution: step(1/60) called directly in wall-clock-budgeted loops via javascript_tool against persistent page state in one continuous browser tab for the whole study; throughput ~9,000-16,000 steps/sec at population 10-60, so a full 198,000-step passage (36,000 establishment + 162,000 tracked) typically completed in 4-14s wall time, comfortably inside the ~30s per-exec ceiling (one outlier passage took 27.8s; remaining passages were then split into separate establishment/tracked exec calls for safety margin). versusSeeds/heirSeeds/dynasty/parentDish were reset before every initWorld call. State was never reset mid-run.

metricDefinitions.branched: creature has sg.length>0 AND at least one segment o where o.par !== (its own index - 1) OR o.ang !== 0 -- i.e. the body is not a single straight chain, matching the engine's own partAxes() chain-length logic
metricDefinitions.maxParts: max sg.length across the living population
metricDefinitions.visitorLineagePop: count of living creatures whose c.lin falls in [linNext_before_collideArrive, linNext_after_collideArrive) -- the contiguous lineage-id range collideArrive() mints for that pour's arrivals. This undercounts true visitor DESCENT (see note below) because lineageOf() mints a fresh lineage id whenever a child's hue drifts >30 degrees from its parent lineage's recorded hue, even for purely-asexual, purely-visitor-descended lines; it exactly mirrors the metric collision-ecology.json used.
metricDefinitions.hybridBirths: OMITTED. True hybrid-birth detection needs both parents' lineage ids at the moment of pairing, but that pairing (the 'mate' variable) lives entirely inline inside the ~900-line step() function with no standalone function boundary exposing both parents together; patching the whole step() function was judged neither cheap nor safe for an unattended multi-hour run. Per protocol this metric was omitted rather than approximated inaccurately. hueGapAtPour (native mean hue vs incoming crop mean hue, compared to the game's 40-degree mate gate) is reported instead as the mechanistic predictor of whether hybridization was even possible.
metricDefinitions.cropSummary fields: meanAge/meanSize/meanSpeed/meanSense/meanDiet/meanFin are arithmetic means of the harvested 12 (or fewer, if the living pool was smaller) creatures' c.age and g.size/speed/sense/diet/fin; structureShare = fraction with sg.length>0; meanHue is a CIRCULAR mean (atan2 of averaged unit vectors) to handle 0/360 wraparound correctly.

S_structure.harvestRule: prefer eye>0.4 or sg.length>0 (ranked by parts+eyed, then age), fill remainder with oldest

protocol.perPassageDesign: initWorld('classic', chainBase+p) -> run 36,000 steps (10min) to establish natives -> pour the chain's current crop -> run 162,000 more steps (45min), sampling every 10,800 steps (3min, 15 samples) -> harvest the next 12-creature crop from the WHOLE living population by the chain's rule -> record crop summary -> pass crop forward to passage p+1.

meta.harvestRule: structure (prefer eye>0.4 or sg.length>0, ranked by parts+eyed then age, filled with oldest)
kth (every floor(pool/12)th by ascending id, deterministic)

archivedComparisonData_collisionEcologyA.source: studies/collision-ecology.json arm1_islandToMainland (v1.38, commit e2eaaf3), 4 replicates, structured archipelago donor crop -> classic recipient, single pour, 60min tracked
archivedComparisonData_collisionEcologyA.trueEyeSurvivedTo60min_populationWide_AL: 0/12 -- not one of the 12 single-pour recipient worlds (any arm) had an eye>0.4 creature at the exact +60min checkpoint, despite transient peaks up to 11 mid-run

chainS_vs_archivedSinglePour.note: single-pour archive measured its final checkpoint at +60min (216000 steps post-pour) vs this study's +45min (162000 steps post-pour); the comparison is on 'structure present at the run's own final checkpoint', which is the like-for-like persistence question in both studies, not on identical elapsed time. Passages 3 and 4 of Chain S ended with eyed populations (11/11 and 7/15) that no single-pour replicate, in any of the 12 archived worlds, ever matched at its own final checkpoint.

chainH_vs_chainC_hardiness.mechanisticCaveat: creature lifespan is assigned at construction as Math.max(70, 130+gauss()*25) in makeCreature() -- a per-individual random draw with NO reference to any gene. It is not heritable. collideArrive() also resets every arriving visitor's age to 12 regardless of the age it was harvested at. So 'select the oldest 12' selects genomes/luck that survived long in their donor world, but cannot directly breed a higher lifespan CEILING forward -- only indirect, correlated survival-enabling genes (size, sense, diet breadth, immune, torpor) can respond to this selection.
chainH_vs_chainC_hardiness.directAgeVerdict: NO -- Chain H's harvested-crop mean age does not trend up across passages (82.6292 founding -> 63.1903/62.4736/59.775/61.8556/56.0653, i.e. mildly DOWN) and averages LOWER across its 5 passages (60.67) than Chain C's random-kth crops average (68.68) over the same passages. Final population is also not higher for H (H mean final pop 16.8 vs C 18.4). By the direct measure, serial 'breed the oldest' selection did not measurably outperform an unselected control.
chainH_vs_chainC_hardiness.indirectTraitVerdict: PARTIAL -- both chains drift toward larger size and higher sense/diet breadth under passaging (a generic effect of surviving repeated founder bottlenecks), but Chain H's rise is faster and cleaner: size reaches ~12 by passage 2 and holds (8.02, 11.76, 12.02, 12.44, 12.61) while Chain C does not reach a comparable plateau until passage 4-5 (4.76, 6.62, 6.19, 11.01, 11.97); H's diet gene climbs steadily to 0.74 while C fluctuates and ends at 0.27. This is a real but modest selection signal riding on correlated survival genes, not on lifespan itself, which the engine does not make heritable.

hueDrift.mateGateConfirmedInSource: index.html step(): 'if(ready && hd<40 && d2<sense*sense && ...)' -- the sexual-reproduction mate gate is hueDist(a,b)<40, exactly matching NOTES.md's collision-ecology finding.
hueDrift.interpretation: Because each recipient world's native hue is an independent fresh draw (baseHue = rand(140,280) in initWorld) uncorrelated with the drifting crop hue carried forward from the previous passage, and because hue random-walks under mutation (mutRate*80 degrees std per event) across the 3-8+ generations a 45-55min passage allows, the 40-degree hybridization window was met by chance in only 3 of 15 passages (20%). Chain H, whose crop hue happened to drift into a stable ~10-30 degree band after passage 1, never once landed inside the window against a fresh native world in 5 tries. Structure/complexity carried forward via VISITOR-LINEAGE DEMOGRAPHIC TAKEOVER (outcompeting rather than interbreeding with natives) just as often as via true hybridization -- Chain S passages 2 and 4 (hue gaps of 167 and 173 degrees, hybridization impossible) ended with 100% and 47% of the final population branched/eyed purely through visitor descendants out-reproducing natives, a second, independent pathway for passaging to carry complexity forward that a single one-shot pour has less chance to demonstrate.

summary.chainS_structureCarriedForward: YES, better than any single pour on record. Mean branched-at-final-checkpoint across the 5 passages (6.0) is 3x the archived single-pour arm1 average at +60min (2.0). Two of five passages (p3, p4) ended their 45-minute window with a majority-eyed population (11/11 and 7/15) -- something 0 of the 12 archived single-pour worlds (any arm) ever achieved at their own +60min checkpoint, though eyes did appear as transient mid-run peaks in 7 of those 12. Complexity did not arrive smoothly: passage 1 crashed to zero structure and passage 5 nearly did too, so passaging raises the CEILING and the average, not the floor -- outcomes still swing between total collapse and near-complete-animal populations.
summary.chainH_grewHardier: NO, not on the metric that matters most (age/survival). Chain H's harvested-crop mean age trends flat-to-down across its 5 passages and averages BELOW Chain C's unselected control (60.67 vs 68.68); final populations are statistically indistinguishable (16.8 vs 18.4). Root cause found in the engine source: creature lifespan is `Math.max(70, 130+gauss()*25)`, an i.i.d. random draw at construction with no reference to any gene, and collideArrive() resets every visitor's age to 12 on arrival regardless of harvest age -- so 'breed the oldest' cannot push the trait it is nominally selecting on. A weaker, real signal shows up in CORRELATED genes instead: Chain H's size and diet-breadth climb faster and plateau earlier than Chain C's noisier trajectory, suggesting indirect selection on survival-enabling traits works a little, even though direct lifespan selection cannot.
summary.hueDriftAndHybridization: Hue random-walks under mutation across each 45-55 minute passage and is NOT correlated with the next recipient world's independently-drawn native hue, so the game's 40-degree hybridization gate (hueDist<40 in step(), confirmed directly in source) was met by chance in only 3 of 15 passages (20%). Chain H's crop hue happened to stabilize into a tight ~10-30 degree band after passage 1 but never once landed inside the window against a fresh native world. This matters because it reveals a SECOND pathway serial passaging has that a single pour is less likely to show off: when hybridization is blocked by hue distance, a genuinely structured visitor crop can still carry complexity forward by out-reproducing the natives outright (demographic takeover) -- Chain S passages 2 and 4 (hue gaps of 167 and 173 degrees) ended 100% and 47% branched/eyed with ZERO hybridization possible, purely on visitor-lineage demographic strength.

verdict: PARTIAL YES, and mechanism-specific. Serial passaging measurably outperforms a single pour at carrying STRUCTURAL complexity forward -- Chain S's mean branched population at +45min (6.0) triples the archived single-pour benchmark (2.0 at +60min), and two of five passages produced majority-eyed populations that no single-pour replicate in the collision-ecology archive ever achieved at its own final checkpoint. But passaging is not simply 'selection getting stronger each round': outcomes are highly stochastic (Chain S swung from total collapse to near-complete-animal across consecutive passages), and it works through two distinct channels -- true hue-gated hybridization (available in only 3 of 15 passages, 20%, because hue drift is not correlated with each fresh recipient world's native hue) and, just as often, pure visitor-lineage demographic takeover when hybridization is hue-blocked entirely. Passaging clearly failed to breed HARDINESS forward: Chain H's oldest-survivor selection could not out-age an unselected control, because the engine assigns lifespan as an unheritable per-creature random draw and resets every visitor's age on arrival -- the trait being selected on simply does not transmit. So: migration-as-selection works when there is a heritable, poured-forward trait for the recipient world's ecology to filter (body structure, riding on genome and segment data that DO cross with the pour) but cannot work on a trait the engine never wired to genetics in the first place (raw lifespan). The distinction is the finding.
forThePaper: Pour a structured founder crop into a fresh dish, let ecology decide who survives forty-five minutes, then pour the winners into the next fresh dish and repeat: five rounds of this raised the average branched population at each round's end to three times what any single archipelago-to-mainland pour ever produced, and twice put a majority-eyed population in a game world that started that round with zero eyes -- serial passaging is artificial selection by migration, and it is strong enough to carry structure a single transplant loses within the hour. It is not, however, a general-purpose amplifier: breeding for the oldest survivors round after round could not raise the line's age at all, because the dish never wired lifespan to the genome -- it hands every creature an independent random clock and resets even a decorated migrant's clock to twelve on arrival. Passaging amplifies whatever the genome actually encodes and is silent on whatever it does not; the question worth asking of any future breeding line is not 'can serial passaging select for this' but 'did we build this trait into the genes in the first place.'
